claim: Expertise in diagnosis rests on stored knowledge structures (encapsulated labels, then illness scripts) more than on better general reasoning; most studies fit the staged account, but evidence is mostly small lab studies.
agent_test: Compare an agent with a stored class library of scripts vs one without, same case set and tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The intermediate effect (mid-level people recall more case detail than experts) appears in several studies (Schmidt and Boshuizen 1993; Rikers 2000; dentistry 2009) but one replication by the same group failed (van de Wiel 1998, recall rose in a straight line). It vanishes with restricted study time and returns only when experts are made to elaborate each finding (Wimmers 2005).
agent_test: Not directly testable on an LLM; use as a caution that recall volume is not a proxy for skill.

claim: Biomedical (causal) knowledge is not discarded by experts; it supports diagnosis, especially after a delay, with unfamiliar terms, and on hard cases. Novices taught causal links kept accuracy better after one week (89% vs 78%).
agent_test: Give the agent mechanism-linked class descriptions vs feature lists; test on delayed or rephrased cases.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Causal learning shows a speed-accuracy crossover: causal learners did better when told to be fast, worse when told to be thorough (71 vs 66; 67 vs 73).
agent_test: Single study with artificial diseases and undergraduates; replicate before use.

claim: Diagnosis also relies on similarity to specific stored cases (exemplars), not only prototype scripts. Combined feature-plus-similarity instructions beat either alone (56% and 53% vs 42% and 41%; N=48 novices, 12 per group, ECG, one lab). Dermatology work puts specific similarity at about 30% of diagnosis. Not tested for LLMs.
agent_test: Retrieval of similar solved cases plus class features vs either alone at equal tokens.
audit_note: Ark, Brooks and Eva 2006 (48 students, 12 per group, 42/41 vs 56/53) and Norman and Brooks 1997 (about 30% in dermatology) verified; Norman, Young and Brooks 2007 is a review from the same McMaster group, so the exemplar evidence is essentially one lab, which the claim already flags.

claim: Interleaved (contrastive) practice across categories beat blocked practice on novel ECGs (46% vs 30%).
agent_test: Order few-shot examples contrastively vs blocked; compare accuracy.

claim: Illness scripts are thought to shift with expertise from Fault (pathophysiology) toward Enabling Conditions (patient features, setting) and Consequences, which are available early and help activate scripts (background in Keemink et al. 2018). A case-based clinical reasoning course raised pre-clinical students' overall script richness by almost 20% (14.47 vs 12.14, n=32) while shifting content toward Enabling Conditions; experts' use of them for first hypotheses was not tested there.
agent_test: Force the agent to extract enabling conditions into the case representation before hypothesising; ablate.
audit_note: Keemink et al. 2018 (32 students) found a case-based clinical reasoning course raised overall illness-script richness by almost 20%, with relatively more Enabling Conditions and less Fault content; it did not teach enabling conditions specifically. Schmidt and Rikers 2007 abstract says nothing on enabling conditions or first hypotheses; the expert-first-hypothesis point appears only as background citation.
claim_before_audit: Enabling conditions (age, sex, risk factors, setting) carry much of illness-script content; experts use them to generate first hypotheses and name more of them. Teaching them raised script richness by about 20%.

claim: Experts categorise patients on deep features (management) more than novices; residents did not differ from experts. Final samples were small (15, 11, 8).
agent_test: Test whether the agent groups cases by management class or by surface features.

claim: Pattern recognition and scheme-inductive reasoning were more often correct than hypothetico-deductive reasoning in think-aloud protocols; correlational and case-dependent.
agent_test: a15 and b12 are the same Coderre 2003 paper, so one source.

claim: Teaching with an illness-script format beat a signs-and-symptoms list on knowledge (15.74 vs 14.38 of 20, p=0.009, d=0.54) and SCT (6.12 vs 4.54 of 10) in a 100-student RCT; one site, three diseases, one session.
agent_test: Format class-library entries as scripts vs flat symptom lists; measure on held-out cases.

claim: Written free-recall scores (accuracy, organisation, encapsulation) track training year, with most growth by year 3 (COPD correct ideas 3 to 14).
agent_test: Snippet-level only; do not rely on it.

claim: Script Concordance Tests give reliable expert-referenced scores with about 100 items and 10-20 panellists, but correlate weakly with factual knowledge.
agent_test: Use SCT-style items to test whether the agent updates correctly when new data arrives.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 0 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: LLM SCT scores rise with model generation: GPT-3.5 8/20, GPT-4 15.6/20, GPT-5 15.2/20 on 20 geriatric items vs 43 experts; on a 750-item benchmark the best model (o3) scored 67.8%, matched students but not senior residents, and reasoning models over-used extreme ratings.
agent_test: Run the agent on SCT items as a calibration probe; expect lower scores than on multiple choice.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 0 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Prompting a model to imitate clinician reasoning modes did not beat plain chain of thought for GPT-4 (Savage 2024: 76% vs 72-78%, n.s.) and hurt GPT-3.5. Related: telling human trainees to use dual-processing did not change the probability of the correct diagnosis in three experiments (Sibbald 2013), and reasoning models did not beat non-reasoning ones at belief updating on real ER cases (ER-Reason). Not yet tested for current reasoning models on NEJM-style cases.
agent_test: One paper (Savage 2024) reported five times. Replicate with a newer model.

claim: Rationale quality is a reliability signal: GPT-4 wrong answers carried false-logic statements in 65% of rationales vs 18% for right answers (n=100).
agent_test: Test a cheap rationale-audit step as a confidence signal.

claim: Frontier LLM differential diagnosis on hard NEJM cases is strong: GPT-4 64% in differential, 39% top (n=70); o1-preview 78.3% in differential, 52% top (n=143); o1 88.6% vs GPT-4 72.9% on 70 shared cases; tuned PaLM2/AMIE top-10 59.1% vs 33.6% for unaided clinicians (302 cases).
agent_test: Use NEJM-style cases; scaffold vs plain model at equal tokens.
audit_note: Kanjee et al. (64% in differential, 39% top, n=70), o1-preview paper (78.3%, 52%, n=143; 88.6% vs 72.9% on 70 cases, where that metric is 'exact or very close') and AMIE DDx paper (top-10 59.1% vs 33.6%, 302 cases) verified; the numbers use different scoring rules across studies.

claim: A role-based scaffold on one model (hypothesis tracker, test chooser, challenger, cost steward) gave MAI-DxO on o3 79.9% at $2,397 vs o3 78.6% at $7,850, ensemble 85.5%; physicians 20%. The accuracy gain on o3 is small; the main gain is cost.
agent_test: Vendor study with no third-party rerun found. Independent benchmark (MedAgentBoard) shows multi-agent systems do not reliably beat a strong single LLM on text QA, and leakage audits show augmented systems can be inflated. Rerun on cases not in any library, at equal tokens.

claim: Giving physicians an LLM did not reliably improve their reasoning: US RCT +2 points (n=50, p=.60); UK replication +8.6 points (74.3 vs 65.7, n=22, p=.001). In both, the LLM alone beat physician plus LLM, partly because users asked it few questions (30%).
agent_test: Matters only for agent-to-human hand-offs.

claim: In BiasMedQA (1,273 USMLE questions, 7 injected biases, 6 LLMs; Schmidgall et al. 2024), GPT-4 scored 72.7% unbiased and lost about 5% on average with a bias cue (worst case -14.0% for false consensus); prompt-level mitigation (education, one-shot, few-shot) gave only modest, uneven gains per bias and generally did not match unbiased accuracy. (Single-paper evidence; the physician automation-bias claim is unsupported and should be dropped.)
agent_test: Inject bias cues; measure whether a challenger step recovers accuracy at equal tokens.
audit_note: LLM part is supported by one paper only (Schmidgall et al., npj Digit Med/arXiv, listed as b23/b24/c04/d21; the other sources are different multi-agent studies). 'Physician automation bias persists after AI training (-14 points)' appears in none of the opened sources; the only 14.0 is GPT-4's worst false-consensus drop. GPT-4 few-shot mitigation (75.2%) actually exceeded the 72.7% unbiased average, though the authors call gains modest.
claim_before_audit: LLM accuracy falls when a case carries a cognitive-bias cue (BiasMedQA, 1273 questions): GPT-4 72.7% unbiased, drop about 5%; prompt-level mitigation recovers only part. Physician automation bias also persists after AI training (-14 points).

claim: Without prevalence cues GPT-4o over-calls rare life-threatening diagnoses (sensitivity 79.3%, specificity 45.2%); adding base rates raised specificity to 83.0% but cut sensitivity to 30.4% (single study). Separately, GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus are weaker on numeric knowledge (how strongly a finding relates to a disease) than semantic knowledge: 56.7-63.7% vs 68.4-68.7%, and doctors scored 82.3% on numeric items (Avnat 2025).
agent_test: Test a prevalence prior in the class library, with a graded rather than binary cue.

claim: GPT-4 wrote illness scripts for 184 diseases: 56.0% sufficient, 15.8% deficient. Cardiovascular (6 of 14) and psychiatric (5 of 11) scripts had the most deficient ratings; dermatology and respiratory had none. The scripts left out symptom frequency and test sensitivity. Whether retrieval from a verified source fixes this was not tested.
agent_test: One paper counted twice. Do not let the agent self-generate its class library unchecked.

claim: LLM-written SCT items and chatbot teaching of illness scripts are judged acceptable (about 90% of criteria met, difficulty the weak point); a chatbot improved script-writing quality in a randomised trial (composite OR 3.2).
agent_test: Mostly small or abstract-only studies; weak support for LLM-assisted knowledge building.

claim: Models given structured retrieval (knowledge-graph paths, disease-retrieval chains with entropy-based question choice) are reported better than plain prompting on their own benchmarks.
agent_test: Scores not recorded. Compare knowledge-graph retrieval with plain retrieval at equal tokens.

claim: Anchoring and premature commitment are common LLM failure modes in clinical tasks: 65.6% of wrong first diagnoses stayed wrong (Braitsch, 32 models); stronger models showed higher bias trap rates on counterfactual pairs (MedEinst, 17 LLMs); over 55% of answers were committed in the first two turns (MINT, 11 LLMs). The earlier 'longer reasoning goes with more errors' point rests on one 100-case study and is not supported elsewhere (see K32).
agent_test: Check whether forced alternative generation lowers anchoring errors.
audit_note: Braitsch (32 models; 212/323 = 65.6%), MedEinst (17 LLMs; paper states stronger models have higher trap rates), MINT (11 LLMs, over 55% in first two turns) and Moell (100 MedQA cases, 7 errors, longer reasoning in wrong answers) all check out. The 'not supported elsewhere (see K32)' part was not checked.

claim: A stored, contrast-organised knowledge base (confusable disease pairs with the finding that separates them, checked against source text) raised LLM diagnosis accuracy over no knowledge, random pages and plain BM25 retrieval. Removing it cut accuracy by 9.0-14.5 points. Not compared with the same tokens spent on free chain of thought.
agent_test: Build a small class library of contrast pairs; compare with free CoT at equal tokens on held-out cases.

claim: Whether a retrieved similar solved case helps an LLM more than a prototype script, and whether the pair is additive as in Ark 2006, is untested. The only related result: adding an exemplar base plus illness graphs to a causal-reasoning agent raised accuracy from 55.49% to 69.49% (MedEinst), but exemplars and graphs were not separated.
agent_test: Four arms: nothing, script only, exemplar only, both; same tokens.

claim: Fixed few-shot examples are an unstable baseline: they were the strongest simple baseline for DeepSeek-R1 on average, but few-shot CoT (14.0%) fell below zero-shot CoT (16.7%) on ER-Reason.
agent_test: Choose examples by retrieval, not fixed; test on a set with a different label granularity.

claim: Gains from challenger, debate and role scaffolds are mostly explained by running several independent proposals. In DMoA the rebuttal stage added about 1-1.5 points over a mixture of 4 proposers; the multi-agent bias study had no single-agent control; MedEinst's debate agents did worse on trap rates. No study matches tokens against self-consistency.
agent_test: Compare challenger step vs plain voting at equal tokens, on cases with a bias cue.

claim: LLMs commit early and rarely recover: over 55% of answers within two turns; salient lab results lure premature answers; deferring the diagnostic question raised accuracy at first commitment by up to 62.6%. Models also can self-correct: wrong-to-right revisions up to 10.6 times the reverse.
agent_test: Force a hypothesis list and a hold step before answering; measure first-commit accuracy.

claim: Reasoning models did not beat non-reasoning ones at sequential belief updating on real ER cases (GPT-5.2 Thinking vs GPT-5.2 n.s.; Claude 4.5 Thinking worse on trajectory). Expert rationales for why a finding shifts the differential raised accuracy for all 8 models.
agent_test: Add expert 'why this shifts the differential' text to class-library entries and test.

claim: The numeric side of a script (frequency, likelihood, sensitivity) is the weak side of LLM-written and LLM-held knowledge: GPT-4 scripts omitted frequency and sensitivity, and numeric QA accuracy lags semantic QA. A graded prior has to be supplied by the scaffold.
agent_test: Store coarse prevalence bands per setting and test for a balanced shift, not the 79% to 30% swing.

claim: More reasoning text did not track better ranking: rubric-rated trace quality correlated only R=0.56 with accuracy, differential reasoning was the weakest component (43.6% vs 66.6% for diagnosis), and MedEinst names 'overthinking' (rationalising an incorrect prior) as a failure mode. No direct LLM test of the human intermediate effect exists.
agent_test: Compare forced-elaboration vs list-then-rank on the same cases.

claim: Reported gains for knowledge-augmented or agent diagnosis systems can be inflated by leakage: strict isolation cut rare-disease Recall@1 from 54.3% to 40.3% (Hedges g=0.94).
agent_test: Hold out cases not present in the library or in public sources.
